title: The Hormuz Blockade Has a Hole. Nearly 3 Million Barrels a Day Are Slipping Through.
excerpt: Ghost tankers with transponders off, Qatari LNG carriers paying tolls, and clandestine dark transits — the supposedly sealed Strait of Hormuz is leaking oil. For India, it may be the difference between a crisis and a catastrophe.
body:
The Strait of Hormuz was supposed to be shut. It is not.

Three months after the US-Israeli war on Iran effectively sealed the waterway that once carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas, a picture is emerging of a blockade riddled with holes. Analysts now estimate that roughly 2.9 million barrels per day of crude made it through the strait in May — far more than the near-zero flows many had assumed.

The numbers come from Piper Sandler's Jan Stuart, who told CNN that about 2.1 million of those barrels moved on vessels that appeared to pay tolls to Iranian entities. The remaining 900,000 barrels came on "ghost" tankers — ships that transited the waterway in the dark with their automatic identification system (AIS) transponders switched off.

"The ghosts, or clandestine flows, help," Stuart said. "There has been far better mitigating of the crisis than I would have thought possible."

## The Toll System That Isn't Official

Iran's ambassador to Moscow, Kazem Jalali, told the Russian newspaper Izvestia on Monday that the Strait of Hormuz would be open "but with new conditions to be determined by the Iranian and Omani authorities." Fees would be charged for transit services, he said, without elaborating.

The statement confirmed what shipping analysts had already observed: Iran has been extracting payments from vessels willing to run the blockade. The toll system is not formalised, and the US vehemently opposes it. President Trump has repeatedly warned that no tolls should be placed on the strait, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Oman's ambassador had told him there were no plans to impose such fees.

Oman, a US ally, has distanced itself from any toll arrangement. But the flows suggest that money is changing hands at sea, regardless of what capitals say on the record.

## Ghost Ships and Dark Transits

The 900,000 barrels per day of clandestine flows represent a significant underground market. These vessels switch off their AIS transponders before entering the strait, making them invisible to ship-tracking services, and reappear on the other side.

Bob McNally, founder of Rapidan Energy Group, told CNN that pre-war Hormuz traffic averaged 125 to 140 daily passages. Current flows are estimated at 0% to 10% of that, but "with this leakage it could be a little higher."

"It's not nearly enough to avoid big and bullish inventory draws," McNally said, "but it does take some of the edge off."

Separately, a fifth Qatari-controlled LNG tanker has transited the strait with a cargo, ship-tracking data showed on Monday. The Al Daayen, controlled by QatarEnergy, loaded at Qatar's Ras Laffan terminal on June 1 and was spotted east of the strait heading for China. An ADNOC-managed tanker, Al Hamra, completed its second inbound dark transit to reload at the UAE's Das Island terminal.

## What It Means for India

For India — the world's third-largest oil importer, which sourced more than 40% of its crude and 90% of its LPG through Hormuz before the war — the leakage is significant. Every additional barrel that makes it through reduces the pressure on India's balance of payments, which has been hammered by a 53% jump in the oil-and-gas import bill.

But it is not enough. India's LPG consumption fell 20% year-on-year in May, the worst supply crisis in decades. Fuel prices have been hiked four times since mid-May. The RBI has unleashed a battery of measures to defend the rupee, including concessional forex swaps for NRI deposits.

The clandestine flows also complicate diplomatic calculations. The US has intercepted 134 ships and disabled seven for non-compliance since its blockade of Iranian ports went into effect on April 13. On Monday, an F/A-18 Super Hornet from the USS Abraham Lincoln disabled the Palau-flagged M/T Marivex after it attempted to enter Iranian waters through the Gulf of Oman — with 24 Indian sailors on board.

The US and Iran have created overlapping, competing blockades. Between them, a grey market has emerged where tankers pay tolls, run dark, or simply take their chances. For India, which depends on this chokepoint for its cooking gas and crude supply, the leaking blockade is better than a sealed one — but a long way from the open shipping lane it needs.
